edges.description: Incomplete apposition and fusion of the optic-fissure margins leaves the persistent ocular cleft that defines coloboma.

The optic fissure runs up to the optic nerve head, so failure of fusion at its most proximal extent leaves a colobomatous defect of the optic disc. This is the mildest end of the MCOPCB13 spectrum, present even in affected individuals whose globe size is normal.
Optic-cup invagination and ventral patterning precede fissure apposition; disturbed cup geometry can therefore compromise the later closure step.
Partial failure of globe morphogenesis produces a small globe.
Severe early morphogenesis failure can prevent globe formation.
Loss of retinoic-acid signaling impairs ventral optic-cup patterning and growth, feeding the shared morphogenesis defect.
Disrupted Wnt/FZD5 signaling, required during eye development, impairs optic-fissure closure and produces coloboma.
Enhancer loss abolishes correct spatiotemporal expression of eye-development genes (e.g. MAB21L2), driving the shared optic-cup and globe morphogenesis defect.
Loss of eye-specific enhancer output lowers IHH expression in the choroid-adjacent cells that supply hedgehog signal to the periocular mesenchyme and retinal pigment epithelium.

Groups several unrelated environmental contributors, including gestational infection and maternal vitamin A deficiency, whose common feature is raising the chance that fissure closure fails rather than a shared mechanism.

The affected dog shows optic nerve head coloboma with choroidal hypoplasia, so it reproduces the failure-of-optic-fissure-closure outcome after a lesion in the same intronic enhancer cluster. It is partial because the canine disease is confined to the posterior pole and does not include the microphthalmia or anophthalmia seen in MCOPCB13.
edges.limitations: The canine lesion is a 7.8 kb deletion of i9, not the human single nucleotide substitution in i8, so it does not model the human allele. The canine deletion's own causal status is contested: it is discordant with the phenotype in some breeds and populations, where it behaves as a linked marker rather than the causal variant. IHH has not been shown to be the canine target; the 2007 report describes the deleted sequence as a conserved protein-binding domain without naming a regulated gene.

nodes.description: Disruption of the eye-development gene regulatory network impairs optic vesicle/optic cup specification, growth, and patterning. Reduced or mispatterned neuroepithelial proliferation yields a small globe (microphthalmia), and in severe cases failure of optic-vesicle outgrowth yields anophthalmia. The same developmental disruption that reduces globe size also predisposes to incomplete optic-fissure closure, so microphthalmia and coloboma frequently co-occur.

nodes.description: The proximate developmental lesion in colobomatous microphthalmia is failure of the embryonic optic (choroid) fissure to close. During optic-cup morphogenesis the invaginating optic cup forms a transient inferonasal groove (the optic fissure) through which the hyaloid vasculature enters; fusion of its margins completes the eye. When fusion fails, tissue is left "missing" at the inferonasal pole, producing coloboma of the iris, ciliary body, retina/choroid, and/or optic nerve. In humans the fissure normally closes by about the 7th week, so the insult is early-embryonic.

nodes.description: Collie eye anomaly is a naturally occurring autosomal recessive canine ocular malformation - choroidal hypoplasia with optic nerve head coloboma - that maps to a homozygous 7.8 kb deletion inside an intron of the canine NHEJ1 orthologue. The human MCOPCB13 report placed that canine deletion on the human genome and found it removes a different member of the same IHH enhancer cluster, i9, where the human variant disrupts i8. The dog is therefore a natural experiment in the same enhancer cluster, at a neighbouring element, with a lesion of a different class.

nodes.description: In microphthalmia/coloboma 13 the initiating lesion is a homozygous deep intronic substitution, NHEJ1 NM_024782.2:c.588+18131A>G, that falls inside a conserved non-coding element of the IHH enhancer cluster named "i8". The element was originally characterised as a limb enhancer; the human variant lies at a position overlapped by a predicted transcription-factor binding motif and by the summit of the chromatin-accessibility peak seen in developing chicken retinal pigment epithelium. Wild-type i8 drives reporter expression in the eye of transgenic mouse embryos at E11.5 and the patient allele does not, so the molecular consequence is loss of eye-specific enhancer output rather than any change to NHEJ1 protein. Because the same cluster remains able to support IHH expression in limb and skull, the expression defect is restricted to a subset of tissues.

nodes.description: A substantial fraction of MAC remains undiagnosed because analysis often focuses on coding variants. Conserved non-coding regulatory elements (enhancers) controlling eye-development genes can be deleted or disrupted, abolishing correct spatiotemporal expression. The ~113.5 kb homozygous deletion 19.38 kb upstream of MAB21L2 removes conserved elements, two of which bind OTX2, and causes microphthalmia and coloboma — establishing enhancer loss as a bona fide MAC mechanism.

nodes.description: IHH is made by non-pigmented cells of the developing choroid next to the retinal pigment epithelium and acts on the periocular mesenchyme and the RPE itself, where it is required for normal RPE pigmentation and for the mesenchymal condensation that forms the sclera. Reduced hedgehog input to that compartment disturbs the retina-periocular mesenchyme interaction on which optic fissure closure depends, which is how a regulatory lesion at the IHH locus reaches the same final common pathway as the coding MAC genes.

nodes.description: Retinoic acid (RA) signaling, generated locally by retinaldehyde dehydrogenases (including ALDH1A3) and acting through retinoic-acid receptors, is required for ventral optic-cup patterning and optic-fissure morphogenesis. Genetic loss of RA synthesis (ALDH1A3) and teratogenic perturbation of the retinoid pathway (e.g. isotretinoin/retinoic-acid embryopathy, maternal vitamin A deficiency) both converge on this pathway, a classic gene–environment phenocopy in MAC.

nodes.description: The Wnt receptor FZD5 is expressed throughout eye development; FZD5 variants disrupt Wnt signaling required for optic-fissure closure. Most reported alleles are dominant-negative (the mutant receptor sequesters Wnt ligands), but a recessive hypomorphic missense allele impairing signal transduction causes syndromic coloboma with microcornea, illustrating an alternative Wnt-pathway mechanism in MAC.
